title: Problem Overview
content: Erdős Problem 121 studies F_k(N), the maximum size of A ⊆ {1,...,N} with no product of k distinct elements being a perfect square. Erdős conjectured F_{2k+1}(N) ~ N; disproved by Tao (2024) for k ≥ 2.
mathContext: This is an extremal problem in multiplicative combinatorics. The structure of perfect squares in multiplicative groups mod squarefree numbers governs which subsets avoid square products. The even/odd dichotomy in k reflects parity phenomena in the group (ℤ/2ℤ)^r of squarefree parts.

title: Perfect Square
content: **`IsSquare n`** holds when n = m² for some m. This is the target property that k-element products must avoid.
mathContext: An integer $n$ is a perfect square iff $v_p(n)$ is even for every prime $p$, where $v_p$ is the $p$-adic valuation. Equivalently, the squarefree part $\mathrm{sqf}(n) = \prod_{p:\, v_p(n)\text{ odd}} p$ equals $1$.

title: k-Square-Free Set
content: **`IsKSquareFree A k`** means no product of k distinct elements of A is a perfect square. For k = 2, this forbids a·b being a square; for k = 3, it forbids a·b·c being a square.
mathContext: Each integer n has a squarefree part sqf(n): write n = sqf(n)·m². Then a₁···aₖ is a square iff sqf(a₁)···sqf(aₖ) = 1 in the group (ℤ/2ℤ)^r of squarefree parts. The k-square-free condition becomes: no k-element subset sums to 0 in this group.

title: Extremal Function F_k(N)
content: **`squareFreeMax k N`** is the maximum cardinality of a k-square-free subset of {1,...,N}. This extremal function is the central object of study.
mathContext: Computing via powerset filtration: check all subsets of {1,...,N}, filter by the k-square-free property, and take the maximum cardinality. Non-constructive in practice, but the definition is clean for stating asymptotics.

title: F_2: Squarefree Density 6/π²
content: F_2(N) = (6/π² + o(1))N: the squarefree integers have density 6/π² ≈ 0.608. A 2-square-free set is exactly a set with no two elements having the same squarefree part.
mathContext: The density 6/π² = 1/ζ(2) arises from the inclusion-exclusion on squarefree numbers. This classical result (Gegenbauer, 1885) gives the exact answer for k = 2.

title: F_3 Has Full Density
content: F_3(N) = (1 - o(1))N: for 3-element products, almost all integers can be included. The density loss is o(1), so asymptotically the full set works.
mathContext: $F_3(N) = (1 - o(1))N$ as $N \to \infty$. The key is that in $\mathbb{F}_2^r$, any 3-element subset $\{u, v, w\}$ sums to zero only if $u + v + w = 0$, and this constraint is sparse enough to allow density 1. Contrast with $F_2(N) \approx (6/\pi^2)N < N$, where the constraint is denser.

title: F_4: Density Goes to Zero
content: F_4(N) = o(N): for 4-element products, the maximum density tends to 0. This stark contrast with F_3 shows k = 4 is the critical threshold.
mathContext: The jump from F_3 ~ N to F_4 = o(N) is a phase transition in multiplicative combinatorics. Erdős expected a similar pattern: F_{even} = o(N) and F_{odd} ~ N. Tao disproved the odd case.

title: Erdős's Conjecture (Disproved)
content: Erdős conjectured F_{2k+1}(N) = (1-o(1))N for all k ≥ 1: odd-index products should allow near-full density. This would mean the even/odd dichotomy persists for all k.
mathContext: The conjecture was natural: for k = 3 (= 2·1+1), full density holds. The surprise of Tao's disproof is that the group-theoretic structure becomes more constrained for k ≥ 5 despite k being odd.

title: Tao's Disproof (2024)
content: **Tao (2024)**: For all k ≥ 4, F_k(N) ≤ (1-c_k)N for some c_k > 0. This disproves Erdős's conjecture for k = 5, 7, 9, ... and shows density is bounded away from 1.
mathContext: Tao's proof uses the polynomial method and character sum estimates. The constant c_k is effective but small. The axiom `erdos121_disproved` records the negation of the conjecture.

title: Monotonicity Properties
content: F_k is monotone in N (more elements available) and anti-monotone in k (more elements required to form a product makes squares easier to avoid). Both are axiomatized.
mathContext: $F_k(N) \leq F_k(N+1)$ (adding an element can only increase the maximum) and $F_{k+1}(N) \geq F_k(N)$ (a $(k+1)$-square-free set is not necessarily $k$-square-free, but the constraint is weaker). Formally: $\{1,\ldots,N\} \subseteq \{1,\ldots,N+1\}$ and any $k$-square-free set is $(k+1)$-square-free.
